intro:
These exercises turn the chapter's central question into practice: for each modeling need, is the set of cases closed and known at compile time, or open and extended later? That one question routes a design to an enum, a struct, a module boundary, or a trait object. The warm-ups make you classify real cases honestly; the implementation and refactoring exercises make you build the closed-set and encapsulation answers; and the design exercise forces you to mix several modeling styles inside one service without pretending one tool is globally best.

The through-line is that Rust separates two concerns a base class used to fuse: reusable data and replaceable behavior. Data reuse comes from owned fields and composition; behavior abstraction comes from traits, with static dispatch by default and trait objects only where one collection must hold heterogeneous implementations. Encapsulation moves from protected members to modules, private fields, and narrow constructors. The lab closes the loop by encoding a document lifecycle as typestate so that invalid states cannot be named at all.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose composition, open polymorphism, or closed polymorphism honestly
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Composition with helper structs and no polymorphism: the reusable retry helper shared by three services. There is exactly one retry implementation; the three services do not need to vary its behavior, only to hold it as a field. A `RetryPolicy` struct owned by each service is the whole answer. Introducing a `Retry` trait here would be a trait with one implementor, which buys nothing and costs a layer of indirection. The honest model is plain composition: each service has a `retry: RetryPolicy` field and calls it directly.

Closed polymorphism with an enum: the fixed set of workflow commands. The variant set is closed and known inside one crate, so an enum (`enum Command { ... }`) plus an exhaustive `match` is the right shape. The compiler then enforces that every command is handled, and adding a command becomes a compile-time repair rather than a runtime surprise. There is no need to box anything or pay for a vtable.

Open polymorphism with a trait: the payment service with swappable fraud checks. There are several semantically real implementations (a rules-based check, a model-based check, a third-party check), and code wants to ask for the capability without naming one concrete type too early. A `FraudCheck` trait with a generic bound (`fn run<C: FraudCheck>(check: &C, ...)`) expresses this with static dispatch where the concrete check is fixed per call site.

Runtime trait objects: the deployment-time plugin registry for exporters. This is the one case that truly needs `dyn`. The set of exporters is open across time and deployment, and a single registry must hold several concrete exporters at once in one collection, selected from configuration. That requires runtime heterogeneity in a homogeneous container, which is exactly what `Vec<Box<dyn Exporter>>` provides. The justification is operational, not abstract: exporters are chosen at deployment, registered into one map, and dispatched at run time, so the choice cannot be resolved at compile time.
criteria: Open vs closed is drawn explicitly: the command set is closed (enum), the exporter set is open across deployment (dyn).
Composition is chosen for the retry helper because no implementation actually varies, so no polymorphism is needed.
The exporter-registry choice is justified by runtime and deployment behavior (one registry holds heterogeneous exporters selected from configuration), not by vocabulary.

exerciseSolutions.title: Collapse an inheritance tree into Rust pieces
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The base class `BaseNotifier` fused two unrelated concerns: shared state (the metrics fields) and replaceable behavior (the act of sending). Rust wants those split. The shared metrics and configuration belong in a composed component, not in a parent type. Model them as a plain struct such as `NotifierMetrics { sent: usize, failed: usize }` (and a separate config struct if there is configuration) that any notifier owns as a field. There is no inherited state and no partially initialized parent, so the metrics object is constructed and tested on its own.

The replaceable behavior belongs in a trait: `trait Notifier { fn send(&self, msg: &Message) -> Result<(), SendError>; }`. `EmailNotifier`, `SlackNotifier`, and `WebhookNotifier` each implement it with their own storage. Crucially the trait carries no data fields, so each implementor chooses its own configuration shape (SMTP host, Slack token, webhook URL) without a shared base forcing a common layout. This is the chapter's point that a trait describes behavior while data reuse comes from ordinary fields.

Notifier selection at the call site depends on the boundary. If a given code path always uses one notifier type fixed at compile time, use a generic bound (`fn dispatch<N: Notifier>(n: &N, ...)`) for static dispatch and zero indirection. If one registry or sink list must hold several notifier kinds at once selected from configuration, that is genuine runtime heterogeneity and wants `Vec<Box<dyn Notifier>>`. If instead the full set of notifier kinds is closed and known in this crate and you simply want to dispatch among them, an `enum Notifier { Email(..), Slack(..), Webhook(..) }` with a `match` is the calmest choice. Choose from the boundary's needs, not from the habit of one base type.

Encapsulation no longer lives in protected fields. It lives in the module boundary: put the metrics struct and the notifier types in a `notify` module, keep their fields private, and expose only constructors and methods. The public surface is the contract; the internal layout stays free to change. That gives tighter encapsulation than a protected-member hierarchy because the exported API is narrower and deliberate.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Shared state composed as a Metrics field; replaceable behavior as a Notifier trait; encapsulation via the notify module.
criteria: Shared state (Metrics) is separated from shared behavior (the Notifier trait) into distinct types.
Traits, composition, modules, and visibility are each used for one job: trait for behavior, fields for state, the notify module and private fields for encapsulation.
Dispatch is chosen from the boundary: a generic bound for the fixed call site, with dyn or enum named for the heterogeneous-registry and closed-set cases.

exerciseSolutions.title: Model closed polymorphism with an enum
exerciseSolutions.solution:
When every variant is known at compile time, the enum is the point. Here a `Transport` enum lists the closed set of transports, and one `dispatch` function handles each variant with an exhaustive `match`. The data for each case lives inline in the variant, so there is no boxing and no pointer chase to reach it, which is the concrete win over a base class plus derived types.

The handler returns a small owned `String` describing what it did rather than logging from inside each arm. That keeps the function pure and testable, and keeps the variant logic in one place where a reviewer can see every case side by side. Returning a value instead of performing a side effect is also what lets exhaustiveness do real work: the compiler verifies the `match` covers the full set.

The exhaustiveness guarantee is the design's backbone. There is no wildcard arm, so adding a `Transport::Quic` variant later does not silently fall through to a default; it produces a compile error at the `match`, forcing a visible repair at exactly the operation that must handle the new case. That is the difference the chapter draws between an enum and trait objects for a closed set: the gain is not just avoiding a vtable, it is exhaustiveness and simpler review.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A closed Transport enum with inline data; one exhaustive match handles every variant with no wildcard.
criteria: The design uses an enum with inline variant data, not Box<dyn Trait>, for the closed set.
dispatch handles every variant with a single exhaustive match.
The match has no wildcard arm, so adding Transport::Quic forces a compile-time repair in dispatch.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair encapsulation after a direct OOP port
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is that the port made every field `pub` so downstream code could mutate state the way subclass code once mutated protected members. A public field is an API promise, not a temporary shortcut: every `pub` field permanently allows outside code to set the value to anything, including states that break the type's invariants. The port effectively published its internal representation as its contract.

The fields that carry invariants must become private immediately. In an `Account`, the `balance`, `currency`, and `id` should be private to the module. They cannot be exposed for direct mutation because outside code could then set a negative balance or change the currency mid-stream, breaking exactly the invariants the type exists to hold. Their values are still useful, so expose them through read-only accessor methods (`balance()`, `currency()`) and a checked constructor (`Account::open`).

Replace direct field mutation with operations that preserve the invariant. Instead of `account.balance = new_value`, provide `deposit(&mut self, amount)` and `withdraw(&mut self, amount) -> Result<(), Error>` that enforce the rules in one place. The externally useful operations survive; only the unchecked write path disappears. Finally, narrow the module surface: rather than `pub mod` over internal submodules, keep the submodules private and re-export only the chosen types and functions with `pub use`, so callers reach a deliberately small API rather than the full internal tree.

This is encapsulation repair, not style cleanup. The change moves representation behind a boundary so the type can keep its invariants and so the internal layout stays free to change without breaking callers. The chapter's framing applies directly: the public surface is the contract, and the internal layout is still allowed to change only because it is no longer part of that contract.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Fields made private, mutation replaced by checked deposit/withdraw, and a narrow public API re-exported.
criteria: Representation fields (id, balance, currency) move behind private visibility and a private internal submodule.
Useful operations survive as a checked constructor and deposit/withdraw methods instead of public field writes.
The change is framed as encapsulation repair: a public field is a permanent API promise, so making it private protects invariants and frees the layout to change.

exerciseSolutions.title: Refactor a state machine into Rust-native transitions
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is a representation that can encode impossible states. With `status: String` plus `approved: bool` and `published: bool`, the type permits combinations the domain forbids: `published = true` while `status = "draft"`, or `approved = false` while `published = true`. The booleans and the string are independent fields, so nothing structurally prevents a contradiction; every consumer must defensively re-check the combination, and a stale write can desynchronize them.

If the value's state varies at run time and the same variable can legitimately be in any state, model it as an enum and let each state carry only the data that state has: `enum DocState { Draft, InReview, Approved, Published { slug: String } }`. Now `published = true while status = draft` is simply unrepresentable, because there is no separate `published` flag; a document is `Published` or it is not, and the slug exists only inside the `Published` variant. Transitions become explicit methods that consume one state and return the next, so the only way to reach `Published` is to call `publish` on an `Approved` value.

Typestate is the stronger choice when the transitions are compile-time linear and the API is the thing you are protecting: each phase is a distinct type (`DraftPost`, `ReviewPost`, `PublishedPost`), and a method that needs a published post takes a `PublishedPost` by type, so a caller cannot even name a draft where a published value is required. The cost is that typestate makes a value's phase part of its type, which is excellent for linear API-facing flows but awkward when something must hold a document of unknown current state in a collection. The chapter's rule decides it: if the same runtime value can be in several states (for example a heterogeneous list of documents in mixed phases), start with an enum; if callers should only ever hold valid phase-specific types across a linear API, prefer typestate.

Either way the redesign prevents the contradiction structurally rather than by validation. The enum prevents it because there is no flag to desynchronize; the slug lives only in `Published`. Typestate prevents it because a draft and a published post are different types, so `published = true while status = draft` cannot be constructed at all.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: DocState enum makes published-while-draft unrepresentable; publish is an explicit Approved -> Published transition.
criteria: Impossible flag combinations are eliminated: there is no separate published flag, so published-while-draft cannot be encoded.
Enum is chosen for the varying runtime value, with typestate named as the stronger option for linear API-facing flows, each with a reason.
The Approved -> Published transition is written explicitly as a method that derives the slug, not as ad hoc field mutation.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose enums, traits, trait objects, and typestate across one service platform
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The pipeline `ingest -> validate -> enrich -> route -> persist -> export` legitimately uses several modeling styles at once. The job of the design is to say which tool fits each boundary.

Closed variant sets, modeled as enums. The fixed set of input commands is closed and known in-crate, so `enum Command { ... }` with an exhaustive `match` drives `ingest` and `validate`. Routing decisions over a known set of destinations are also enum-shaped (`enum Route { Persist, DropInvalid, Quarantine }`). The domain justification is that these sets are defined by the system's own contract, not by third parties: a new command is a deliberate change to the platform, and exhaustiveness turns that change into a compile-time repair across every handler rather than a runtime gap. The data for each command lives inline, so there is no boxing on the hot ingest path.

Open plugin seams, modeled as traits and trait objects. Exporters are pluggable and chosen at deployment, and one registry must hold several concrete exporters at once, so the `export` stage uses `trait Exporter` with a `Vec<Box<dyn Exporter>>` registry. This is the runtime-dispatch boundary, and its justification is operational: exporters are registered from configuration at startup, the set differs per deployment, and a single loop must drive all of them, which cannot be resolved at compile time. Where a stage instead has a single implementation fixed per build (for example the `enrich` enrichment source in a given binary), a trait with a generic bound gives the same abstraction with static dispatch and no vtable.

Plain composition, no polymorphism. The `persist` stage and the pipeline wiring itself are mostly composition: a `Pipeline` struct owns a validator, an enricher, a router, a persistence handle, and the exporter registry as named fields. None of those need to vary polymorphically just to be held together; they are dependencies the pipeline owns directly, visible and individually testable. Cross-cutting helpers such as the retry policy and metrics recorder are likewise composed fields, not a base class.

The operator rule workflow (author -> review -> publish) is a closed, linear, API-facing lifecycle, which is the strongest case for typestate: `DraftRule`, `ReviewRule`, `PublishedRule` as distinct types, so a function that activates a rule can require a `PublishedRule` and a draft cannot be passed where an active rule is expected. If instead operators browse a mixed list of rules in varied phases, an enum state is the better fit because one collection holds values in several states; the deciding question is whether callers hold one rule through a linear flow (typestate) or a heterogeneous set at once (enum).

Observability and testing hooks fall out of these choices. The enum command and route sets get exhaustive state tests, so a new variant fails the build until its handling and its test exist. The `Exporter` trait gets a plugin contract test that every registered exporter must pass (same input, asserted output shape), since the set is open and only the contract is guaranteed. And because routing and lifecycle transitions are explicit enum or typestate moves, each transition can emit a structured event, giving an event log that renders the document's path through the pipeline for after-the-fact debugging.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Commands and routes as enums, exporters as a dyn-trait registry, and the pipeline as plain composition of owned fields.
criteria: Enums own the command and route sets, the Exporter trait object owns the plugin seam, and plain composition owns the pipeline wiring.
The exporter registry is justified operationally: heterogeneous exporters registered from configuration at deployment and driven by one loop.
The command and route enums are justified in domain terms: a contract-defined closed set whose extension is a deliberate compile-time repair.
Observability and testing hooks are named: exhaustive state tests for enums, a plugin contract test for exporters, and per-transition event logging.

labSolution.explanation:
The scaffold already encodes the lifecycle as typestate: `DraftPost`, `ReviewPost`, and `PublishedPost` are three separate types, and the only way to move between them is the consuming transition methods `request_review` and `publish`. Each method takes `self` by value, so the previous state is moved out and can no longer be used; a draft cannot be published directly because there is no `publish` method on `DraftPost`, only on `ReviewPost`. That makes invalid orderings unrepresentable at compile time rather than guarded at run time.

The only missing piece is in `publish`: the original code left the slug empty, which would make `published` print `false`. The fix derives the slug exactly where the `PublishedPost` is constructed, by lowercasing the title and replacing spaces with hyphens, so `"Rust OOP"` becomes `"rust-oop"`. Because this is the sole construction path for a `PublishedPost`, the type can never exist with an empty slug, which is the typestate guarantee carried into the data itself.

In `main`, `published = !published.slug().is_empty()` is therefore `true`, and `published.slug()` is `"rust-oop"`, producing the two expected lines. The `let _ = published.title();` line simply reads the retained title so the field is used; the program compiles cleanly with only the standard library.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the difference between open polymorphism and closed polymorphism in Rust design?
reviewAnswers.answer: Closed polymorphism means the full set of cases is known at compile time inside one crate, so it is modeled with an enum and an exhaustive match; adding a case becomes a compile-time repair across every match. Open polymorphism means the set of implementations is extended later or across crates and deployments, so it is modeled with traits, using generic bounds for static dispatch or trait objects when one collection must hold several implementations at run time. The deciding question is whether the set of cases is closed and known, or open and extended over time.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does composition usually replace inheritance for shared state and shared helpers?
reviewAnswers.answer: Rust has no class inheritance with shared fields, so a type cannot extend another to inherit state; instead a struct owns the components it needs as named fields. Composition grows data sideways as fields you can name, swap, and test one at a time, rather than downward through a chain of parents with hidden inherited invariants. This removes fragile base classes, partially initialized parent state, and unclear aliasing across broad object graphs, and it keeps every dependency visible, testable, and replaceable, including in tests that substitute one component.

reviewAnswers.question: When is `dyn Trait` the honest runtime model instead of an enum?
reviewAnswers.answer: Use `dyn Trait` when the system needs genuine runtime heterogeneity: one collection or registry must hold several concrete implementations at once, and the set of implementations is open across time and deployment rather than fixed in one crate. Typical cases are plugins, strategy registries, sinks, and handlers selected from configuration, where the concrete type cannot be known at compile time. If instead the set of cases is closed and known, an enum is better because it keeps every case in one type, stores data inline without boxing, and gives compiler-checked exhaustiveness.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are enums and typestate often better than classical state-pattern objects in Rust?
reviewAnswers.answer: A lifecycle is a closed set of states with a finite list of legal transitions, which an enum models directly with match arms that the compiler checks for exhaustiveness, so adding a state forces a visible repair everywhere it is handled. Typestate goes further by making each phase a distinct type, so a caller cannot even name a value in the wrong state, eliminating impossible combinations at compile time rather than guarding them at run time. The classical state pattern models each state as a boxed object behind an interface, which is still correct but needlessly dynamic when Rust's enum and typestate alternatives give stronger static guarantees with no boxing.

reviewAnswers.question: Where does encapsulation usually live in Rust if not in a base class hierarchy?
reviewAnswers.answer: Encapsulation lives in modules, private fields, narrow constructors, and focused methods. The module boundary hides the representation, private fields keep invariants enforceable, and the exported API is the contract while the internal layout stays free to change. This often gives tighter encapsulation than a deep protected-member hierarchy because the public surface is narrower and more deliberate, and a module can re-export only the chosen types with `pub use` rather than exposing its internal submodules.
